nameStory: The Thick-lipped Drill gets its name from two distinctive features that make it a formidable hunter of the sea floor. Its shell opening has a noticeably thickened, rolled lip that looks like it's been reinforced, while 'drill' refers to its amazing ability to bore perfectly round holes through the shells of clams and other mollusks using its specialized feeding structure. This little sea snail is essentially a living power tool, drilling through prey shells to reach the soft meat inside!
description: The Thick-lipped Drill is a small to medium-sized sea snail that lives along New England's rocky shores and sandy bottoms. Like other murex snails, it has a sturdy, spiral shell with a pointed spire and distinctive sculptural ridges or bumps running along its surface. The shell typically ranges from grayish-white to brown in color, and the thick, flared lip around the opening is its most recognizable feature. These are active predators that hunt other shelled creatures on the ocean floor.

idTips.label: Thickened Shell Lip
idTips.description: The shell opening has a distinctly thick, rolled outer lip that feels substantial and reinforced when you run your finger along it - much thicker than most other small sea snails

idTips.label: Spiral Shell Shape
idTips.description: Cone-shaped shell with 5-7 whorls that taper to a pointed spire, feeling solid and heavy for its size

idTips.label: Surface Sculpture
idTips.description: Shell surface has raised ridges or bumps (called axial ribs) running vertically that you can feel with your fingertip, giving it a textured, non-smooth surface

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Usually grayish-white to brownish, sometimes with darker banding, and often has a weathered, chalky appearance when found on beaches

idTips.label: Size Range
idTips.description: Typically fits comfortably in your palm, smaller than a golf ball but larger than most periwinkles you'd find on the same beach

habitat: Look for Thick-lipped Drills in shallow coastal waters from the low tide zone down to moderate depths along New England's rocky shores and mixed sand-shell bottoms. They're often found among mussel beds, oyster reefs, and areas with plenty of clams and other bivalves that they prey upon. You're most likely to find empty shells washed up on beaches after storms, particularly on shores with nearby rocky subtidal areas.

seasonality.spring: Active hunting season begins as waters warm. Fresh shells with intact animals may wash up during spring storms, and this is when they're most actively drilling holes in prey shells.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're actively feeding and reproducing. Look for them in tide pools and shallow water during very low tides.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to slightly deeper water. Good time to find shells on beaches as storm activity increases.
seasonality.winter: Mostly in deeper water avoiding harsh conditions. Winter beach walks are excellent for finding well-preserved empty shells that have washed ashore.

funFact: A Thick-lipped Drill can drill a perfectly round hole through a clam shell in just a few hours using a combination of acid secretions and a rasping tongue covered in tiny teeth - it's like having a biological drill bit and chemical solvent all in one, and the holes they leave behind are so precise they look machine-made!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other small whelks or moon snail shells, but the thick, rolled lip is the dead giveaway - run your finger around the shell opening and if it feels like it has a reinforced rim, you've found a drill. Moon snail shells have thin lips and are usually much smoother overall.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'drill' for these snails comes from their predatory behavior, not their appearance, which can be confusing since the shell itself doesn't look like a drill bit. They're part of the murex family, which includes some of the most elaborately spined shells in tropical waters, though our New England species are much more modest in their ornamentation.
compareHints: Since this is the only Eupleura species commonly found in New England waters, compare it with other murex family members like dogwinkles, which have thinner lips and more pronounced spiral ridges. Thick-lipped Drills are generally more robust and heavy-feeling than dogwinkles, and lack the sharp spiral cords that make dogwinkles feel rough to the touch. The thick lip is really the distinguishing feature that sets this species apart from other predatory snails in our region.
